text: Did the student personally do something that caused all their selected courses to disappear from their enrollment?
Were the courses lost because of a technical or system problem with the university's course selection platform?
Did another person intentionally remove or take the student's courses?
Did this other person know the student personally, such as a friend, classmate, or roommate?
Was the other person able to remove the courses because they had access to the student's account credentials?
Was the removal done through the university's official course selection system by someone with administrative authority, such as a staff member?
Did the student tell someone their course choices or schedule, and that person used that information to interfere?
Were the courses removed because the student was dropped from them by a process that the other person triggered, rather than by the person directly editing the student's enrollment?
Did the other person take the student's course places for themselves by enrolling in the same courses?
Was the interference physical rather than digital — for example, taking or destroying the student's enrollment materials or device?
Did the student voluntarily give their course selections over to the other person as part of a permitted arrangement, such as letting someone else use their course quota?
Was the other person the student's course instructor or professor?
Did the other person act out of malice or a grudge against the student?
Was the other person acting to help or benefit the student, rather than to harm them?
Did the other person believe the student's chosen courses were a mistake or unsuitable for the student?
Did the other person remove the courses to help the student meet a deadline or rule, such as by clearing the student's schedule so the student could re-enroll properly?
Was the other person closely associated with the student's university enrollment, such as an academic advisor or tutor?
Was the other person acting on behalf of the university in some capacity?
Did the other person take over the student's account or identity to submit the course selection on the student's behalf, believing it would help?
Did the other person's helpful action involve the student's course selection being submitted or confirmed earlier than the student intended?
Did the student's courses disappear because the courses themselves were cancelled or removed from the university's offerings?
Was the other person a family member or someone acting on the family's behalf?
Did the helpful interference involve money or payment, such as the other person paying for the student's courses?
Did the other person swap or exchange the student's courses with other courses, so that the student ended up enrolled in different courses than intended?
Did the other person release or drop the student's course places so that they would become available to other students, believing this would help the student?
Was the other person a computer program, bot, or automated tool rather than a human?
Did the other person take the student's courses as part of a plan to give the student better courses, which the student then failed to get?
Was the other person a friend or classmate who was also a student at HKU?
Did the other person's helpful action involve transferring the student's course places to the student's benefit in the future, such as reserving them for a later term?
Was the student required to select courses in multiple rounds, and did the other person's action cause the student to miss a round?
Did the other person gain access to the student's course selection because the two shared a computer or were logged into the same account?
Did the other person's action cause the student's courses to be dropped because the student was deemed to have exceeded a course or credit limit?
Did the other person enroll the student in the courses themselves — that is, was the student's course selection made by this person without the student's knowledge?
Did the other person help the student by reminding or prompting them about a deadline, and the student then lost the courses for another reason?
Did the other person take the student's courses to use them as a bargaining chip or to trade them back to the student?
Was the other person a parent or guardian who intervened in the student's enrollment?
Did the other person mistakenly believe they were helping the student when they removed the courses?
Did the other person intend to help the student in a way unrelated to the student's courses, and the course loss was collateral damage?
Did the other person's helpful intention concern the student's schedule overall — such as reducing the student's workload?
Did the other person remove the courses as a prank or joke they thought the student would find funny?
Did the courses disappear because they were added to the student's cart or a temporary holding area rather than being confirmed, and the other person's helpful action was meant to fix this?
Was the student's enrollment compromised because the other person shared or posted the student's login details, intending to help by getting others to enroll the student?
Did the other person take the student's courses so that the student would be free for something else — such as a trip, event, or opportunity arranged to help the student?
Did the other person pay or bid on the student's behalf, such that the courses were dropped when the bid or payment failed?
Was the other person a teacher or tutor who, intending to help, told the student to drop their courses and take different ones?
Is the other person someone with whom the student had a close personal relationship, such as a romantic partner?
Did the other person take the courses from the student so they could be given to someone else in need — for example, a student who was unable to enroll?
Did the courses disappear as a result of the student's account being merged, transferred, or converted — for example, when the student's enrollment status changed?
Did the other person act to help the student avoid a conflict, such as a timetable clash?
Was the other person a staff member in the university's course selection or registration office acting informally to help the student?
Did the other person help the student by taking the courses in exchange for something the student wanted, such as a swap done with the student's agreement but misunderstood?
Did the other person remove the courses because the student had asked for help in a way the other person misinterpreted?
Did the other person take over the student's course selection because the student was unable to complete it themselves — for example, due to illness or absence?
Is the "other person" a system process at HKU, such as an automated add/drop or waitlist function, that a person set up intending to help the student?
Did the other person add courses to the student's schedule in a way that exceeded the maximum allowed, causing the system to drop the student's courses?
Did the other person's helpful action cause the student to be flagged as having an unpaid balance or unmet condition, resulting in the courses being removed?
Was the student's course selection lost overnight because the other person intentionally dropped the courses to help the student change their major or program?
Did the other person take the student's courses as part of helping the student to graduate or fulfill a requirement?
Did the other person remove the courses so that the student could be offered courses the other person had secured for them?
Did the other person take the student's courses as a favor so that the other person could then swap in courses the student actually wanted?
Did the other person remove the student's courses to help the student win a scholarship, competition, or other opportunity?
Did the other person take the student's courses so the student could take a leave of absence or exchange program that would benefit them?
Was the other person trying to help the student by making the student's courses available to the other person, with the intention of sharing notes or materials?
Did the other person intend to help the student by enrolling the student in courses taught by the other person or by someone the other person trusted?
Was the other person acting to help the student in a context involving the student's mental health or wellbeing?
Did the other person take the student's courses so that the two of them would have the same schedule?
Was the other person a rival or competitor of the student, such as someone competing for the same limited course places?
Did the other person's action involve transferring the student's course selection to a different account or program, with the intent of helping the student?
Did the other person remove the courses to help the student get a refund of tuition or course fees?
Did the other person remove the courses so that the student could be re-enrolled through a special arrangement the other person had made, such as an exchange or special admission?
Did the other person act to help the student by removing courses that the student had enrolled in but could not attend due to a schedule conflict with a mandatory activity?
Was the other person's helpful intent to assist the student with a course selection that the student had attempted but that had not gone through correctly?
Did the other person cause the courses to be dropped by mistakenly applying a "drop all" or reset function while trying to help the student?
Did the other person remove the student's courses in order to help the student avoid failing or being disqualified?
Did the student ask the other person for help with course selection, and the other person's helpful attempt went wrong?
Did the other person take the student's courses because the other person wanted the student to spend more time with them or on a shared activity?
Did the other person remove the student's courses to help the student by giving them a lighter semester during a difficult time?
Did the other person take the student's courses as a side effect of a legitimate administrative or personal action they took with good intentions, not directed at the courses themselves?
Did the other person claim the student's course places for themselves with the intention of later giving the student a better schedule?
Did the other person take the student's courses in order to help the student by holding or reserving them until the student was ready to take them?
Did the courses disappear because the other person, intending to help, logged into the student's account and accidentally submitted or confirmed a change that removed the courses?
Was the other person a representative of the student's sponsor or government body administering a scholarship, acting to help the student comply with scholarship rules?

Did the other person take the student's courses so that the student would be forced to take a course the other person was teaching or recommending, which the other person believed was better for the student?
Did the other person take the student's courses to help the student by enabling the student to avoid a course they would have failed or disliked?
Was the other person the student's thesis supervisor or research mentor, acting to help the student focus on research instead of coursework?
Did the other person take the student's courses in order to help the student secure a place in a course with limited capacity, by freeing up the student's schedule?
Did the other person remove the student's courses in order to help the student by preventing the student from being over-enrolled, a situation the other person expected to be corrected later?
Did the courses disappear from the student's view because another person moved them into a different category or waitlist within the system, intending to help?
Was the other person a representative of a student society or club who took the student's courses to help the student participate in an activity?
Did the other person remove the student's courses because the student was about to be penalized for an enrollment violation, and the other person was trying to shield the student?
Did the disappearance of the courses involve the student's course selection being reset to a default or previous state by a helpful person?
Did the other person take the student's courses in exchange for payment or a bribe, believing it would help the student financially?
Was the other person the student's academic advisor acting to help the student adjust their study plan?
Did the other person take the student's course places so that the student could be placed in a combined or double-degree program that the other person believed would benefit the student?
Did the courses disappear because the student's enrollment was changed by someone intending to help the student qualify for a student visa, scholarship, or financial aid condition?
Did the other person take the student's courses to help the student by keeping the student under a certain credit load required for a benefit?
Was the other person a member of the student's household who removed the courses to help the student by giving them more free time, and the student then failed to re-enroll in time?
Did the other person take the student's courses to help the student switch into a program or courses that would start immediately, leaving the student's original schedule empty?

Did the student's courses disappear because the student had enrolled in them but a person with the student's cooperation (intending to help) dropped them so the student could re-select courses in a later enrollment period, which the student missed?

Another person intentionally removed all of the student's enrolled courses, and that person was acting to help the student rather than to harm them. The removal was not done through the official course-selection system by a staff member or administrative authority, was not a system/platform failure, was not the courses being cancelled, was not a physical interference, and did not involve the other person gaining access through shared credentials or the student's account being taken over. The student did not personally cause the loss, did not provide their schedule for interference, and the courses were not taken by the other person enrolling in them, swapping them, reserving them for later, or paying/bidding on them. So the surviving causal story is: someone connected to the student, meaning to benefit them, caused the student's entire set of course enrollments to be dropped in one evening; the student had not intended or personally effected this, and the help backfired, leaving the student with no courses by the deadline.
